While it mentions God treating the midwives well (וַיֵּ֥יטֶב אֱלֹהִ֖ים לַֽמְיַלְּדֹ֑ת - 'God dealt well with the midwives'), this passage is entirely silent regarding God's empathy or lack thereof toward the Israelite people. The passage describes the Israelites multiplying and thriving (וַיִּשְׁרְצוּ וַיִּרְבּוּ) despite oppression, but does not explicitly state God's emotional disposition toward them at this point in the narrative. Furthermore, the midwives are not 'Hebrew leaders' in the traditional sense—they are professional attendants. The claim that God 'does not have empathy for the people' contradicts the text's silence on this matter and anticipates theological developments that come later in Exodus (such as God hearing the people's cries). The text provides no textual basis for this negative characterization.
